messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 65-year-old married man who has spent years working on the floor of a large retail store, where he helps customers, restocks shelves, and spends long shifts under bright lights and near the automatic front doors. He traces the change in himself to a hurricane that tore through his neighborhood two years ago. During the storm, the power failed in the middle of the night and the house seemed to shake around him. He and his wife moved from room to room listening to windows rattle and objects strike the siding, trying to judge whether they would need to get out. What stayed with him most was the feeling of being trapped while the danger closed in from all sides, scanning in the dark for the quickest way out if the roof gave way. Even after the storm passed, he had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that surviving had not left him relieved so much as altered; in his mind, he had permanently changed for the worse, into someone who could never again afford to let his guard down.

That belief hardened over the following months. Kwame was certain he now had to be on guard all the time, and this conviction shaped how he moved through ordinary life. At work, the first thing he did on entering the break room, stockroom, or sales floor was locate the nearest exit. He positioned himself so he could stay close to a door, and while talking with customers he found his eyes moving past their faces to doorways, corners, and signs of possible danger. He distracted himself by fussing with tasks, straightening displays repeatedly or focusing on small bits of restocking, because if his mind went quiet the storm came back too vividly. In his own understanding, these habits were necessary; if the world was dangerous and he was no longer the man he used to be, staying near an exit and constantly checking his surroundings felt like the only sensible way to get through the day.

His memories of the hurricane are not like a story he can tell from start to finish. He describes them as a film that plays over and over: the shriek of wind, the darkness after the power cut, the sense that the walls might split. When it comes back, he does not feel that he is remembering something finished. He feels as if it is happening right now. In those moments the event seems present rather than past, and that immediacy drives home his belief that danger is everywhere and that something in him has been permanently damaged. The memory itself becomes proof, to him, that he has not truly come through it.

Because the memories arrive with that force, his body and attention stay keyed up. At night he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to remain alert, as though sleep would leave him unprepared for the next disaster. Entering any room, even a familiar one, he scans for exits almost automatically. He is superalert, watchful, on guard. The reverse is true as well: the more vigilant he becomes, the more likely he is to catch some small cue—a hard rain against the store windows, a sudden dimming of lights, the slam of a loading-bay door—and the film starts again. On the sales floor during thunderstorms, he can feel himself pulled out of the present and back into that night, his chest tight, his mind insisting that what happened before could happen again at any moment.

This constant sense of threat has steadily narrowed his life. Staying close to exits and checking the environment give him a brief feeling of control, but they also keep confirming his view that danger is always near. When he sees himself unable to stand in the middle of a room without plotting an escape route, it seems to him further evidence that he has changed for the worse. The same pattern plays out at work: because he is scanning so intently, he rarely feels settled with customers, and he often shifts his position to keep a clear path to the door. He distracts himself to get through his shift, yet the effort of doing that leaves him exhausted and no less watchful. Each precaution tells him the danger must be real; each night of lying awake on alert convinces him again that the world is unsafe.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was worn down by the sense that the hurricane had never really ended inside him. His wife had begun to notice that even at home he was always checking where the exits were and rarely relaxed enough to fall asleep easily. He came to treatment because he was frightened by how present the storm still felt and by what that seemed to say about him. More than anything, he fears that this guarded, altered version of himself is permanent, but he is also hoping, cautiously, that he might learn how to live in a room without first preparing to escape it.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in any single paragraph that Kwame’s negative beliefs or appraisals directly lead to or intensify the trauma memory.
